notes:
I couldn't find everything you asked for. Most of these notes come from Enduring Word (David Guzik), John Chrysostom's sermons on newadvent.org, Sam Storms, GotQuestions, and the older commentaries on Bible Hub and StudyLight. I found nothing from Lutheran, Orthodox, Anglican, Wesley's own notes, or prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace sources, so those are left out. The Methodist view comes only from Adam Clarke. Verses with no entry are verses I didn't find covered.

**1 Corinthians 14 – Research notes**

**v. 1**
- Traditional reading: JFB says love should be the first and main aim, because 13:13 calls it "the greatest." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/1_corinthians/14.htm
- Guzik: wanting gifts was fine. The Corinthians' fault was turning that wish into an obsession, while love should be the main pursuit. The church was putting too much weight on tongues and too little on prophecy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/
- **Where traditions differ (what "prophecy" means):**
  - Cessationist (believes the miraculous gifts have ended): GotQuestions treats prophecy as "speaking forth," not necessarily predicting, and links it with preaching. On this reading, tongues is a lesser gift than prophecy, because preaching God's Word builds up believers and tongues does not. https://www.gotquestions.org/cessationism.html
  - Continuationist (believes the gifts continue today): Guzik says the cessationist reading reduces prophecy to "inspired preaching." He replies that Paul did not use the usual Greek word for preaching (*kerusso*). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**vv. 2–3**
- Guzik: a tongue is speech addressed to God, not to other people. The most serious misunderstanding is to treat tongues as a supernatural message from one person to another. He adds that people who think the miraculous gifts have ceased have trouble with this verse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/
- Guzik on "mysteries": sounding meaningless to listeners does not make it gibberish. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/
- Guzik on prophecy: it is directed to people and is mostly positive. It builds up, encourages and strengthens. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/
- JFB, following Bengel, says the two main kinds of building up are exhortation, which shakes off sluggishness, and comfort, which lifts sadness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/1_corinthians/14.htm
- Chrysostom, the 4th-century preacher (hosted on a Catholic site and honoured by Catholics and Orthodox alike): saying that no one understands lowers the gift, but "mysteries in the Spirit" raises it again, so it does not look useless. Both gifts come from the Spirit, but prophecy also helps the hearers. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220135.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Paul is not scolding people for "self-edification." He is describing how the gift works. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/
- Chrysostom: here Paul means speakers who understood their own words but could not pass them on to others. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220135.htm

**v. 5**
- Chrysostom: "rather" and "greater" show that prophecy ranks higher, not that tongues is opposed. Paul is not belittling the gift but leading them on to something better. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220135.htm
- Guzik: Paul valued tongues for his own prayer life. In the meeting prophecy is greater, but in private prayer tongues would be more useful, since there is no one to prophesy to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**v. 6**
- Guzik: Paul names four kinds of understandable speech: revelation, knowledge, prophecy and teaching from Scripture. Each could help others because it was in a language everyone knew. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**vv. 7–9**
- Guzik: like a flute played out of tune or a trumpet with an unclear call, tongues in the meeting "speak into the air." Hearing tongues may satisfy curiosity but does not build anyone up spiritually. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**vv. 10–11**
- Guzik: language is God's gift and part of being made in his image. Because every language has meaning, God understands a tongue even when the speaker does not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**vv. 12–14**
- Guzik: the aim of the meeting is to benefit one another, so a tongue needs an interpretation. An interpreted tongue helps others the way reading a Psalm does: they overhear someone's prayer to God and can agree with it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/
- Guzik on v. 14: in tongues the spirit prays while the mind is left out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**vv. 15–17**
- Guzik: "singing with the spirit" can mean using tongues in melody during worship, but never in a way that draws attention or distracts. Paul here makes reference to how we can sing in the spirit. God can give us the freedom to exercise the gift of tongues in a melodic way, so it flows in with worship. However, based on the principles in this chapter, if this is done, it should never be done in a way that would draw attention to itself or distract others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/
- Storms (charismatic) on the "Amen" in v. 16: a good interpretation turns the unclear tongue into something clear enough for the whole church to say "Amen" to. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/interpretation-of-tongues--judging-prophetic-words---and-women--1-corinthians-14:26-40-

**v. 18**
- Guzik takes this verse to mean Paul could probably speak in tongues whenever he wanted. He calls it a "hint," not a clear statement. Paul said in 1 Corinthians 14:18, "I thank my God that I speak with tongues more than you all." That's a hint; it's not a clear statement. But it seems to indicate that Paul could speak in tongues whenever he pleased. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/correcting-my-mistakes-qa-for-january-6-2022/

**v. 20**
- Chrysostom: children chase trifles. The Corinthians treated the "lowest" gift as if it were everything. They should be innocent like children toward evil but mature in understanding. He links this to Matthew 10:16, "wise as serpents, harmless as doves." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220136.htm
- Guzik: the Corinthians were being childish and selfish by building themselves up at others' expense in the meeting. In their selfish desire to edify themselves at the expense of others in the meeting, the Corinthians showed themselves to be children, and selfishly immature. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**v. 21**
- Chrysostom: Paul often uses "the Law" for the whole Old Testament; this quotation is from Isaiah. "Not even thus" shows the miracle was enough to amaze, so the blame for unbelief lay with the hearers. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220136.htm
- Barclay: in Isaiah, Israel's disobedience brought Assyrian conquerors whose language they could not understand. Even that did not turn them back to God. Because of their disobedience, the Assyrians will come and conquer them and occupy their cities and then they will have to listen to language which they cannot understand. They will have to listen to the foreign tongues of their conquerors speaking unintelligible things; and not even that terrible experience will make an unbelieving people turn to God. So Paul uses the argument that tongues were meant for a hard-hearted and unbelieving people and were, in the end, ineffective to them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/14-22.html

**v. 22 (much debated)**
- **Sign of judgment:**
  - Gill calls tongues a sign of wrath and punishment inflicted on a rebellious and unbelieving people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/14-22.html
  - Bible Hub's study notes connect the verse with Isaiah 28:11–12, where foreign tongues were a sign of judgment on unbelieving Israel. This aligns with the Old Testament prophecy in Isaiah 28:11-12, where foreign tongues were a sign of judgment to unbelieving Israel. https://biblehub.com/study/1_corinthians/14-22.htm
- **Sign that wins converts:**
  - Clarke (Methodist): the gift was not for those who already believed. It was meant to show unbelievers that the work is God's, so they would accept the gospel. The miraculous gift of tongues was never designed for the benefit of those who have already believed, but for the instruction of unbelievers, that they might see from such a miracle that this is the work of God; and so embrace the Gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/14-22.html
  - Lyth (19th-century sermon notes): tongues are proof of God's power, for the unbeliever who needs it. Tongues a sign — not for the believer who did not require it, but for the unbeliever, as a proof of Divine power. https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_corinthians/14-22.htm
- **Sign that amazes:**
  - Chrysostom: "sign" here means something that astonishes rather than teaches. Prophecy helps both believers and unbelievers. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220136.htm
  - Calvin agrees and cites Chrysostom: tongues were meant to fill unbelievers with astonishment, not to teach or reform them. Here Chrysostom starts a question' "If tongues were given to unbelievers for a sign, why does the Apostle say now, that they will be derided by them?" He answers, that they are for a sign to fill them with astonishment — not to instruct them, or to reform them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/1-corinthians-14.html
  - Calvin also says the Corinthians used tongues out of place and neglected prophecy, which was meant for believers. Hence, the Corinthians brought forward that gift improperly and out of its right place, allowing prophecy in the meantime to be neglected, which was peculiarly and specially set apart for believers https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/1-corinthians-14.html
- **Cessationist:**
  - GotQuestions reports that cessationists use this verse to argue tongues warned the Jews of judgment for rejecting Jesus as Messiah. Using this verse, cessationists argue that the gift of tongues was a warning to the Jews that God was going to judge Israel for rejecting Jesus Christ as Messiah. https://www.gotquestions.org/gift-of-tongues.html
  - GotQuestions' separate article on this verse says the gathered church does not need a sign meant for unbelievers. The gathering of believers has no need of the sign for unbelievers. https://www.gotquestions.org/tongues-are-a-sign-for-unbelievers.html
- **Continuationist:** Guzik admits the verse is hard. He suggests tongues may be a negative sign of judgment, as the Assyrians' language was in Isaiah's day. Either way, tongues do not draw unbelievers closer to God. Perhaps Paul is saying that tongues are indeed a sign to unbelievers, but not a positive sign. They are a sign of judgment, as the unknown tongues of the Assyrians were in Isaiah's day. So, while we may not exactly understand what Paul means by tongues are a sign, not to those who believe but to unbelievers, we know he does not mean tongues "minister" to or edify unbelievers. Tongues do nothing to bring the unbeliever closer to God; they may instead turn him off. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**v. 23**
- Chrysostom: the charge of madness comes from the outsiders' ignorance and unbelief, not from the gift itself. Compare Acts 2:13, where some thought the apostles were drunk. Paul's point is to push the Corinthians to look for an interpreter and to stop showing off. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220136.htm

**vv. 24–25**
- Chrysostom: prophecy lays bare the secrets of a person's heart, which is far more awe-inspiring and useful than hearing strange languages. He gives Peter exposing Sapphira as an example of prophecy at work. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220136.htm
- Guzik: Paul shows that prophecy helps unbelievers and uninterpreted tongues do not. So, in 1 Corinthians 14:23-25, Paul seems to indicate that tongues are not beneficial in ministering to unbelievers, while prophecy is beneficial to unbelievers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**v. 26**
- Guzik: Paul pictures a meeting where people come to take part and give to one another, not just to receive. Paul sees the gathering of the church as a time when people come to participate and to give to one another, not merely to passively receive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**vv. 27–28**
- Storms:
  - It is unclear whether "two or three" means for the whole meeting or before each interpretation; he leans to the whole meeting.
  - "In turn" corrects people speaking all at once.
  - Speakers should know beforehand whether an interpreter is present.
  - Without one, the gift belongs to private prayer.
  - Interpretations of tongues should be addressed to God (prayer, praise, thanks), so be cautious with "messages in tongues" aimed at the congregation. He notes this differs from a long Pentecostal assumption that an interpreted tongue works like prophecy.
  https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/interpretation-of-tongues--judging-prophetic-words---and-women--1-corinthians-14:26-40-
- Guzik: v. 28 shows the speaker controls the gift. The Spirit does not force anyone to speak out. Paul here makes it plain that the gift of tongues is under the control of the person with the gift. They are not "compelled" by the Holy Spirit to speak out in tongues. If there is no interpreter present, the tongues' speaker is fully able to keep silent in church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**v. 29**
- Storms:
  - Prophecies should be tested against Scripture, whether they build up, the test of love, the wider community, and experience.
  - "The others" who weigh them are probably the whole congregation.
  - Congregational prophecy may mix revelation with human interpretation, which is why it must be weighed.
  - Prophesying falsely is not the same as being a false prophet.
  https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/interpretation-of-tongues--judging-prophetic-words---and-women--1-corinthians-14:26-40-
- Guzik: prophecy is also regulated. Worship and the Word are the centre of the church's life, not the gifts. The gifts of the Spirit are never to be made the focus of congregational life. Worship and the Word are the focus, and the gifts flow under God's direction around the focus of worship and the Word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**vv. 30–32**
- Guzik: no one is "overwhelmed" by prophecy; the speaker stays in control. The goal is learning and encouragement, and gifts with no such fruit are pointless. Here, Paul makes it plain that no one is "overwhelmed" by prophecy. They are still in control of the exercise of the gift, even when the Holy Spirit is moving upon them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-14/

**v. 33**
- Storms: "as in all the churches" belongs with v. 34, not with "God is not a God of disorder." Paul often backs his rules with the practice of all the churches, and the other reading would be a trite remark. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/interpretation-of-tongues--judging-prophetic-words---and-women--1-corinthians-14:26-40-

**vv. 34–35 (the most debated verses)**
- **Strict silence:**
  - Barnes (Presbyterian) calls the rule positive, explicit, and universal: women were to take no part in public teaching, and not even ask questions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/14-34.htm
  - Gill (Baptist) reads it as an exception to "all may prophesy" (v. 31), aimed at women preaching in Corinth. This is a restriction of, and an exception to one of the above rules, that all might prophesy; in which he would be understood of men only, and not of women https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/1-corinthians/14-34.html
- **Silent unless divinely prompted:**
  - The commentary placed under the Geneva Study Bible heading on Bible Hub: women were silent unless they had a special revelation, which fits 11:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/14-34.htm
  - Clarke (Methodist): Paul banned women arguing doctrine with men in public. But if God specially moved a woman to teach, she was not barred from obeying. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/14-34.html
- **Silence about judging prophecy:**
  - Bible Hub's commentary: the silence concerns the public floor, such as teaching or judging prophecy (v. 29). https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/14-34.htm
  - Storms lists and weighs the main options:
    - A later scribal insertion: he rejects it.
    - Paul changed his mind: a few liberal scholars hold this.
    - 11:5 does not really approve women speaking.
    - Different kinds of meetings.
    - Only wives are meant.
    - Women were disrupting the service: he rejects this, asking why Paul would silence all women and no unruly men.
  https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/interpretation-of-tongues--judging-prophetic-words---and-women--1-corinthians-14:26-40-
  - Carson (Reformed; TGC/bible.org) also rejects the "noisy" and "uneducated" explanations. were too noisy cannot be taken very seriously, for we must ask why Paul [forbid]s all women from talking. And were there no noisy men? Nor is it plau[sible that] the women are silenced because they were uneducated https://media.thegospelcoalition.org/documents/carson/1991_silent_in_the_churches_1Cor_14.pdf
- **Women did speak in Jewish settings:** Beecher's sermon (19th century) argues that outside the synagogue's liturgy, Hebrew feeling favoured women speaking out, and that these limits applied to Greek churches. https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_corinthians/14-34.htm
- **Modern scholarship (were vv. 34–35 part of the original letter?):**
  - The facts: no manuscript leaves the verses out, but the Western group of manuscripts places them after v. 40. Gordon Fee argues they were added later. many of the Western witnesses have these verses after v. 40, while the rest of the tradition retains them here. There are no manuscripts that omit the verses. https://bible.org/article/textual-problem-1-corinthians-1434-35
  - Carson calls Fee's view "weak and speculative." https://bible.org/book/export/html/2821
  - Philip Payne argues that a scribal mark in Codex Vaticanus, an early manuscript, shows the scribe doubted these verses. https://bible.org/series/c
  - The NET Bible note suggests Paul himself probably wrote the words in the margin. it is likely that Paul himself added the words in the margin. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=1Co&chapter=14&verse=35
  - GotQuestions: the evidence for keeping the verses after v. 33 is "overwhelming." https://www.gotquestions.org/1-Corinthians-14-34-35.html

**vv. 36–37**
- Carson: vv. 37–40 still deal with tongues, prophecy and authority in the church, which tells against moving vv. 34–35. Verses 37-40 are still demonstrably talking about tongues, prophecy, spiritual gifts, authority in the church—the very topics that have dominated chapter 14. https://bible.org/book/export/html/2821
- Storms: one argument for the interpolation view wrongly treats the "or" at the start of v. 36 as rejecting vv. 34–35. No other use of that word in Paul works that way. this view requires taking the Greek conjunction e ('or,' left untranslated in the NIV) at the beginning of verse 36 as a complete repudiation of what has gone before, even though no other use of e in Paul functions in that way. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/1-corinthians-14:34-35

**vv. 38–40:** I found no commentary on these verses in the pages I could read.
